implementation_notes: Swift's standard library puts the fold on the Sequence protocol: reduce(initialResult, nextPartialResult) combines the elements with a closure and returns initialResult for an empty sequence, and because it is declared rethrows a throwing closure makes the fold throwing with no extra spelling. The monoid cases have their own members (min/max, joined, first(where:), contains(where:)), which are preferable where they fit; sequences that are single-pass (AnyIterator, a file or network reader) can only be folded once, and there is no built-in right fold - a right-associative combine over a bidirectional collection goes through reversed() or a recursive function. The hand-written structural form remains a recursive function that switches over an enum's cases, which is how a tree or expression type is consumed.
pitfalls: The accumulator is a value: every step returns a new one, so folding into a copy-on-write collection with the value-returning form copies once the buffer is shared, turning a linear fold into a quadratic one (use reduce(into:) for that carrier).

There is no seedless reduce: an empty sequence returns initialResult, so a min/max fold seeded with 0 reports 0 instead of signalling emptiness - the specialized Sequence.min()/max() return an optional for exactly this reason.

A closure that mutates captured state is a side effect hidden inside an otherwise deterministic fold, and it cannot be reused for a concurrent or async traversal; thread the accumulator through the return value instead.

variants.name: reduce(into:) - in-place accumulation into a mutable carrier
variants.implementation_notes: reduce(into:) takes an inout accumulator and an update closure that mutates it (func reduce<Result>(into initialResult: Result, _ updateAccumulatingResult: (inout Result, Self.Element) throws -> ()) rethrows -> Result), so a Dictionary, Array or Set accumulator can be mutated in place instead of rebuilt - which is the difference between linear and quadratic behaviour for copy-on-write carriers, since the value-returning form shares the buffer and copies on the next step. Choose it whenever the carrier is a mutable collection or the update is naturally an append/insert/merge; keep the value-returning reduce when the carrier is a scalar or when purity of the combining function matters more than the copies, because the inout form hides mutation inside the fold and makes the step a procedure rather than a function.
pitfalls: The update closure is a procedure, not a pure function: it cannot be reused as an algebra for a lazy or parallel fold, and testing it means observing the mutated carrier rather than comparing return values.

The two spellings are not interchangeable for copy-on-write carriers: reduce with a Dictionary/Array accumulator that appends each step copies the buffer until it becomes uniquely referenced, which is the classic quadratic flattening trap that reduce(into:) documents its way out of.

Inout mutation makes the closure's effect on the carrier opaque at the call site, so the accumulator's final shape must be understood from every branch of the closure - an argument for a small named function when the update logic grows.
